title: The Dog Ate My Homework: Education's Evidence-Excuses Echo Chamber
author: Snow, Pamela
source: The Next 30 Years by Robert Pondiscio (Substack)
summary: Cognitive psychologist Pamela Snow catalogs and systematically refutes 16 recurring arguments that educators use to resist evidence-based practice. The article, published in Robert Pondiscio's newsletter, diagnoses education's unique capacity to generate "permission structures" for ignoring research—a pattern Snow calls the evidence-excuses echo chamber. She documents how familiar refrains ("every child is different," "teachers need autonomy," "context matters too much") function not as legitimate objections but as rehearsed deferrals that insulate ineffective practices from accountability. Snow argues that medicine, aviation, and engineering accept evidentiary standards that education routinely refuses; and that this double standard has real victims in classrooms. The essay closes with a challenge: professional judgment matters, but it must be grounded in—not used as a substitute for—the best available evidence.
points: Education's evidence-excuses are rehearsed, not reasoned: Snow identifies 16 recurring deferrals that function as a collective permission structure to maintain ineffective practices regardless of evidence.

The autonomy argument is frequently weaponized: teacher professional autonomy is legitimate, but claiming it as a shield against evidence is a category error—no professional field grants autonomy from evidence.

Every child is different is true but irrelevant as an objection: group-level research identifies what works across populations, and the variation argument doesn't negate the baseline benefits of evidence-based approaches.

Education has uniquely low evidentiary standards compared to other professions: Snow notes that medicine, aviation, and engineering all accept research-derived practice standards without the reflexive resistance that characterizes education.

Victims of the echo chamber are concrete: when schools resist structured literacy because of "professional judgment," children who would have learned to read do not—this is not a philosophical disagreement but a practical harm.
quotes: She turns her attention to another vexing and enduring feature of the education landscape: our remarkable capacity to generate excuses for ignoring evidence.

Snow examines the familiar refrains—'every child is different,' 'experience matters more than research,' 'evidence threatens teacher autonomy'—that allow ineffective practices to persist long after the evidence against them has become clear.
Pam's argument is not that professional judgment doesn't matter. Rather, she asks why education so often grants itself exemptions from the standards of evidence we readily apply elsewhere.
It would seem of the maxim that when you stand for nothing, you fall for everything. But education is, ironically, a slow learner.
The obligation now is to keep saying clearly what is being lost before the generation that never learned to read inherits the consequences.
